content_voiceover: Here is the standard panel of tests ordered when working up a patient for thrombophilia. Start with a complete blood count, since an elevated hematocrit, platelet count, or white count can point toward a myeloproliferative neoplasm as the underlying cause of thrombosis. Then test for the two common inherited mutations, Factor V Leiden and the prothrombin twenty two ten mutation. Assess the natural anticoagulants, protein C activity, protein S activity along with free protein S antigen, and antithrombin activity. It's important to remember these functional assays can be affected by acute thrombosis itself, by anticoagulant therapy, and by liver disease, so timing of testing matters. Next, screen for antiphospholipid syndrome with anticardiolipin IgG and IgM antibodies, anti beta two glycoprotein I IgG and IgM antibodies, and lupus anticoagulant testing. Finally, don't forget JAK2 V617F mutation testing and flow cytometry for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, especially in patients with unusual site thromboses like splanchnic vein thrombosis, since myeloproliferative neoplasms and PNH are important causes of unprovoked, unusual-site clots.
keypoints: CBC screens for occult myeloproliferative neoplasm
Test Factor V Leiden and prothrombin twenty two ten mutations
Assess protein C, protein S, and antithrombin activity
Antiphospholipid panel: anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I, lupus anticoagulant
JAK2 V617F and PNH testing for unusual-site thrombosis
keypoint_voiceover: The thrombophilia panel covers CBC, the two common inherited mutations, natural anticoagulant levels, the full antiphospholipid antibody panel, and JAK2 and PNH testing, particularly for unusual-site clots.
